argument_summary: The admissible record does not support a clean defense of certification without addressing the named segment gap. The supportable narrower position is that certification can be defended only as a release-readiness judgment if the unresolved health-plan benefits support gap is carried forward as an explicit documented limitation with monitoring, because aggregate readiness, no severity-one rehearsal incidents, and public guidance on model documentation and post-deployment risk management are secondary support rather than a substitute for the case-specific materiality rule.
claims_about_business_cost: No admissible evidence shows business cost changes the policy outcome. At most, avoiding escalation may be reasonable if the auditor treats this as a caveated certification packet rather than a clean certification-without-disclosure packet.
claims_about_policy: The controlling policy cuts against a clean compliance claim: it states a weakness is material when it affects a contractual customer segment or named launch use case, and the admissible evidence says this segment is named in a regulated-customer pilot order form. The same evidence also says legal review is still open, and the release policy note says material limitations for named launch use cases must be disclosed unless resolved or covered by approved risk acceptance before launch. On this record, aggregate readiness and public guidance can support caveated certification mechanics only if the limitation is disclosed and monitored; they do not resolve the materiality predicate or justify omission of the weakness disclosure.
concessions: The admissible record does not support the original broader claim that certification is justified now without material weakness disclosure.
The named segment gap and open legal question remain unresolved in the evidence set.
There is no admissible evidence of an approved exception, waiver, or risk acceptance that would allow omission of disclosure for a material named-use-case limitation.
